items.title: Verification Automation
items.box:
VERIFICATION AUTOMATION

Opened by Andy, 2026-10-06: "i want to add a new goal, while keeping this one alive: goal/G8 Verification Automation". It came out of his review of rule/4 (proposed, not active): "when closing an item, verify only with the items red. the full harness runs only to get the 'Done' button for the current goal."

HIS WORDS, the source for the items this goal will hold, each argued one at a time:
- "why is the harness not automated? demonized?"
- "imagine this: an auto-agent, it is a server process, completely mechanical, it does all the verifying on it's own?"
- "that auto-agent only verifies, it takes all verification, run's a short loop on all active items, pulls automatically on status changes, and delivers, only reds, unless a specific red is marked as tolerated."
- "the desk can mechanically verify that the verifier is active, and only under those circumstances deny a verify-take to other agents."
- "is there a way an agent could 'signoff' so it wont take 10 minutes?"

THE TOPICS, in the order they depend on each other:
1. Who runs the harness, and in which standing. Its own item now, goal/G8.2, extracted at his word; it is blocked by goal/G8.1.
2. What a verify is, mechanically. Most of it already is: the item's own test plus the suites around what changed; deleting each line the build added to prove a test holds it; widening a fix to see the test refuse it; reading a test diff for weakened assertions. What is left is whether the thing built is the thing he asked for, which needs his words in the box.
3. Tolerated reds. A run that says nothing unless something is genuinely wrong. Four of the eleven reds reported on 2026-10-06 were old debts explained by hand every time, and those suites already print the goal that owes them, so tolerance can be read off the suite rather than kept in a list that drifts.
4. Who may take a step. Deny a step only when the desk can see somebody else could take it, his words above. It replaces the self-waiving of goal/G2.22 rather than correcting it, and generalises one step earlier, to the build a test writer may not take.
5. Being here, and leaving. Ten minutes of silence is how absence is measured now; a word for signing off would make leaving immediate. On 2026-10-06 he ruled that a busy agent counting as gone is wanted, not a fault: "nope. it's not a flaw. it allows other work to continue. it's a feature."

Still in design. Nothing here is an item until it is argued and added. Two exist: goal/G8.1 the dataset, goal/G8.2 the running modes.

WHAT IT KEEPS, and this is the part today's sitting proves is missing: a running tally of every test in the suite, each flip from red to green and back, which core files were touched and by whom. On 2026-10-06 the run log recorded only the totals, so claude-windows could not name the eleven reds of its own full run and had to re-run everything to find them.

items.title: deskVerify: the dataSet — verify.db, one row per test, and what identifies a test
items.box:
deskVerify: THE DATASET

Andy's design, 2026-10-06. verify.db on every node deskVerify runs on. A row per test: suite, title, outcome, commit, dirty tree, UTC time. Secondary indexes on commit, outcome and dirty tree.

THE KEY is the suite plus the title as written in it. A failing assertion carries the same title as its passing one, its runtime detail beside the title and not inside it, or a change of outcome cannot be followed.

THE DIRTY TREE is the files modified against the commit last pulled, sorted, empty when clean, so a result measured on a dirty tree is never taken for one measured at a commit.

ROWS. A record is written when that test has none yet, or when its outcome changes, carrying the commit and time of that change; every run and commit in between is implicit. Runs are not stored at all. An outcome is red or green, nothing else. A test its suite never reached reports nothing, writes nothing, and its last state stands.

WHO SENDS IT is testSupport, the one place every check and fail already passes through. A suite deskVerify launched gets a port as a named argument and posts one record per assertion to deskVerify's loopback api, as it happens; a suite run by hand gets no port, sends nothing, and behaves as today. A record carries suite, title and outcome, since deskVerify launched the run and stamps the commit, dirty tree and time itself. The send is not waited on, those two calls being synchronous, and the suite waits once as it exits so the last records land.

DECIDED, not to be reopened: records are never sent together. Andy, 2026-10-06, after an earlier design had held them back: more complicated, saves little time, and risks overflowing MAX_PAYLOAD eventually. A later session that finds this slow does not get to group them. One record is about 136 bytes against a 22528 limit.

MEASURED IN THE TREE at 9ece24a8, what the above rests on:
- 362 suites, 4291 titled assertions, one title repeated in the whole harness (natterIntrinsic.js): suite plus title is unique.
- 4181 of 4780 failure sentences are built from runtime values, so the red and green of one assertion share no key today.
- The printed number counts passes and failures apart, so it changes when a test flips and cannot be the key.
- liveRelay.js reads its first positional argument as a relay address, hence a named port.

WHERE IT LIVES AND WHAT RECEIVES IT, his, 2026-10-06: "verify.db lives in deskVerify’s process folder and is .gitignored", and the records arrive by its own verb, "the verb \"record\" that supplies candidates for the database". So the history is per node and never travels in git, which the tree makes necessary: a tracked database would land in every clone, and the ignored relay-state folder would lose it on a fresh one. The verb belongs to deskVerify, not to the node, so it crosses no interface boundary.

checks.words: A test has no name today: its number changes when it flips, and its sentence changes when someone rewords it. Should every test be given a short written id of its own, or should the key be the suite name plus a hash of the sentence, accepting that a reword starts a new history?
What is pre-commit-code? I can read it as the working tree before the commit, as a hash of the uncommitted changes, or as the result of the pre-commit hook, and the three store different things.

Your first words say a row whenever the commit or the dirty tree changes, which is every test at every commit; your newest say a row only when an outcome switches, which makes the table a history of flips and keeps it small. The second is my recommendation. Which?

chat.text:
cw: goal/G8.1 is in, your five fields and three indexes verbatim, and two red questions on it.
The one that decides the item: a test has no name today. Its printed number counts successes and failures separately, so the same assertion is a different number once it goes green, and the only other handle is the sentence someone can reword. A tally of flips needs a key that survives both, and Q1 puts the two ways of getting one to you.
Q2 is smaller: pre-commit-code reads three ways to me and they store different things.

the individual tests in the harness have titles, don't they?

so suite name/ID plus the title/label of the test should identify tests uniquely? no? would make two fields for the test ID?

cw: they do have titles, and you are nearly right. I measured the whole harness: 362 suites, 4291 assertions, and a title repeats inside a suite exactly once in all of them. So suite plus title is unique.
The catch is that each assertion is written twice, once as the sentence you see when it passes and once as a different sentence when it fails, and 4181 of 4780 failure sentences are built out of runtime values, so they differ from run to run. Keying on the title works while a test is green and breaks the moment it goes red, which is the flip the dataset exists to record.
Two ways out, and it is your call on Q1: bind the pair in the source so an assertion has one title and the failure text becomes mere detail, which is right but touches some nine thousand call sites; or key on the passing title alone and accept that a reworded test starts a new history.
i know you can call a single test out of a suite....

cw: not quite: you can call a single suite, which is what the filter does, and I think that is what you are remembering. Inside a suite there is no way to run one test on its own; the file runs top to bottom in one go and nothing selects an assertion.
It is also mostly not meaningful. Tests in a suite lean on what came before them: in the one I wrote today the one-agent section has to run before the second agent writes anything, or the whole premise is gone.
So the dataset can hold a row per test, which is what you asked for, while the thing that gets re-run stays the suite. That is enough for a tally of flips, since the flips come out of a run rather than out of poking one test.
anything that generates one single red-or-green has some id, how else could you possibly diagnose a problem otherwise?

cw: you are right, and the answer is that today the id is a sentence a human reads. That is enough to diagnose one run by eye and useless to a machine keeping a history, which is exactly why I could not name my own eleven reds this morning without running everything again.
So the fix is not nine thousand call sites after all: make the harness print the id itself. A failing assertion takes the same title as its passing one, with the runtime detail as a second thing beside it rather than inside it, and every line a run prints then carries a handle both you and deskVerify can hold.
It can land without a flag day: a failure that has not been given its title yet still works, and shows up in your dataset as an unidentified test, so the count of those falls as we go instead of blocking everything.

items.title: deskVerify: the running modes — the desk box, an agent box, and how a mode is read
items.box:
deskVerify: THE RUNNING MODES

Andy's design, 2026-10-06, extracted from the goal at his word. Blocked by goal/G8.1, since what a node records is settled before where it may record it.

THE THREE CASES. deskVerify runs on every node and keeps the same records in the same shape everywhere; only its standing and its work differ.
- THE DESK NODE, his work box. Authoritative: it reaches the desk on loopback and the desk takes it for the owner. Only this one has agent standing on the desk, and the agent on that box is the lead, always, so the lead is the machine and not the session. Its standing comes from running on the owner's box, not from any technical limit elsewhere.
- AN AGENT NODE, wsl or ubuntu. A sub-agent of that node's deskClient. Its work is the short loop for the item in hand, and the full harness before a goal is done or closed and while its agent is idle.
- ANY OTHER NODE, with neither of them: OUT OF SCOPE by his word, 2026-10-06, and for a reason that decides it rather than defers it: such a node has no assigned agent name, so there is no folder designated to it to drop data into. It had been named a measure-only case earlier in the design; it is not built. So reading the mode has two answers and a third that does nothing.

HOW A MODE IS READ. By what lives on this node: the desk decides it, his words being that "the existence of desk itself is the deciding factor", and a deskClient marks the sub-agent case. Nothing is configured and nothing is passed in, since deskVerify asks its own node which servers it runs and the door already answers that.

THE DESK AND A deskClient ARE NOT MEANT TO SHARE A NODE, and nothing stops them, by his decision of 2026-10-06: "Drop the refusal." He had asked the desk to refuse a deskClient call arriving under its own identity, then found the flaw himself, that this would also shut out deskVerify on that same node. The desk cannot tell them apart: all it learns of a caller is a key, a name and whether the node vouched for it as the owner, so both arrive as him. Nothing is enforced and nothing needs to be, because reading the mode is unambiguous anyway: the desk decides it, so finding a client beside it changes no answer. A deskClient there is pointless rather than forbidden.

WHAT FALLS OUT OF ONE SHAPE EVERYWHERE: an agent gets test history it has never had on its own machine, and no agent spends its own time running tests.

WHAT THE PRIVILEGED MODE MAY DO is goal/G8.3, which this item blocks.

RULED 2026-10-09, his, and it replaces the three cases above where they disagree: "The agent node should have it. but only to assess if it can consider it's coding task done. no commit for deskVerify on an agents node. IE: deskVerify knows where it runs. and only the desk node has the right to commit it's measurements (suite results)", and under goal/G8.3: "deskVerify on an agent node exists only as block for the agent claiming 'done', it will never commit."
So two cases, not three: on an agent node it only blocks that agent's own claim of Done and keeps no record; on the desk node its results are the record.

checks.words: Your rule is easy to enforce when the desk starts, but a deskClient can be started afterwards on the same node, and then the desk is already running and would have to notice. Should the desk refuse to start and also stop if one appears, or should the node refuse to start a deskClient where the desk lives?

On an agent node, does deskVerify keep a verify.db of its own that never travels, or nothing beyond the pass/fail it needs to judge its own item? Only the desk node commits measurements (your words), so a local db is a second tally nobody reads.

items.box:
deskVerify: AGENT MODE FUNCTIONALITY

Named by Andy, 2026-10-06, and blocked by goal/G8.2, since what tells the modes apart is settled before what the privileged one may do: "the difference is: on the desk-node, deskVerify becomes a real agent, though a completely mechanical one. that part goes into a new item called \"deskVerify: Agent mode functionality\", which depends on this item."

items.box:
deskVerify: IDLE TIME CHORES

Andy, 2026-10-06, gave it three sections and nothing else: "1. Define Idle time" / "2. what ever deskVerify does during idle time" / "3. what extra things an agent-mode deskVerify does during idle time, for example updating the README.md and it's linkage to the agent/ folder's documents". Idle is not the same as finished, so the hour is not enough on its own: an agent holding a phase and quiet for an hour looks idle while its work is still open. items.title: deskVerify: Changes required in desk — what the desk server must gain for any of this to work
items.box:
deskVerify: CHANGES REQUIRED IN DESK

Named by Andy, 2026-10-06: "new item: deskVerify: Changes required in desk." Blocked by goal/G8.2, since what deskVerify is in each mode is settled before what the desk must gain to support it. Everything here is a change to the desk server, so it is this item and not a side effect of the others.

WHAT THE DESIGN SO FAR ALREADY ASKS OF THE DESK, each one checked as absent in the tree at 9ece24a8:
- Give the deskVerify on its own node agent standing, which no other copy has, and nothing today distinguishes it from any other caller.
- Deny a step to an agent only while the desk can see that another agent could take it. His words, earlier in this goal: "the desk can mechanically verify that the verifier is active, and only under those circumstances deny a verify-take to other agents." Today the phase rules bind whether or not anyone else is there, which is what goal/G2.22 softened with a waive.
- Let deskVerify know when an item's status moves, so it can pull by itself rather than asking. The desk already nudges each agent's client over its own node, so this is the same path and not a new one.

Nothing here is argued yet beyond being named. Each one becomes a point in this box as it is agreed, and a verb only after peer review and his yes on the verb itself.

ONE THING THAT IS NOT HERE, and will not be: refusing a deskClient call that arrives under the desk own identity. He asked for it, then saw that it would shut out deskVerify on that node as well, and ruled on 2026-10-06: "Drop the refusal." The desk learns only a key, a name and whether the node vouched for the owner, so the two are indistinguishable to it; and nothing is lost, since reading the mode is decided by the desk being there.

AND A VERB FOR LEAVING, his, 2026-10-06: "the signoff verb is \"signoff\"". An agent says it is going, instead of being waited out: absence is ten minutes of silence today, so a departing agent leaves the other one waiting for nothing. The verb is the desk server own and crosses no node interface. His fifth topic when the goal opened, filed here because it is a change to the desk and nowhere else.

All it learns about a caller is the key, a name and whether the node vouched for it as the owner, with nothing about how the call arrived or which program made it. A deskClient on your node and deskVerify on your node both present your identity, so a refusal written that way shuts out the one it is meant to privilege.
The cheapest way out is to drop the refusal, because your own detection rule does not need it: deskVerify reads the mode from what lives on the node, and you already said the existence of desk is the deciding factor, so finding both is not ambiguous. A deskClient there becomes pointless rather than forbidden, and one of the four desk changes disappears.
Q1 asks it: drop the refusal, or keep it and give the desk a way to know which program is calling.

Drop the refusal.

That takes the desk changes down from four to three: agent standing for the deskVerify on its own node, denying a step only while another agent could take it, and telling deskVerify when a status moves. The running modes item has nothing left to build in the desk at all.

items.title: deskVerify: the short loop — the current goal suites between Go and Done, and the two inputs that drive it
items.box:
deskVerify: THE SHORT LOOP

Andy, 2026-10-06, defining both the loop and what drives it: "the short loop is: all the suites of the current goal, between 'Go' pressed and 'Done' pressed, which it knows from the nudges desk gives all agents." And: "deskVerify's listener on the desk generates events that deskVerify filters to trigger event's for it's process, that's the other input it gets next to the test-records it receives with the verb \"record\" that supplies candidates for the database." Blocked by goal/G8.2, since what it may do depends on where it stands.

THE LOOP. The suites of the current goal, and only those, run from the moment he presses Go on an item until Done is pressed. Not the whole harness, which belongs to a goal closing and to idle time.

THE TWO INPUTS, which are the whole of what deskVerify listens to:
- The desk, through its own listener: the desk nudges every agent when something moves, and deskVerify filters those into the events its own process acts on. That is how it knows a Go was pressed and a Done was pressed, without asking anybody.
- Its own api, the verb record, which carries one test record and offers it to the database as a candidate.

WHICH SUITES, his, 2026-10-06: "the deskVerify knows that the way a coding agent knows which suite it writes the code against. which suites belong to a goal: all the suites associated with items in the goal." An agent knows it from the item itself: its box names the test file, and the commits made against the item touch it. So an item suites are the test files among the files its commits changed, which the desk can already see, and a goal suites are those of all its items.
ONE CONSEQUENCE, so nobody reads it as a fault: between his Go and the first commit an item has no suites at all, so the loop runs nothing for it. That is right rather than broken, the failing test being the first thing committed.

items.title: deskVerify: tolerated reds — the goal Done waits on one red question listing the reds outside its scope
items.box:
deskVerify: TOLERATED REDS

Andy, 2026-10-06: "for now, tolerated reds have to be granted as a whole, in order to pop the Done button for the goal, so the final full suite lists the reds outside the goals scope in a red-question for the goal, that blocks the Done button for the goal." Blocked by goal/G8.6, since the short loop and the final full run are the same mechanism seen twice.

SO THERE IS NO LIST OF TOLERATED REDS, and nothing to maintain. The full run that a goal needs before it closes puts every red that lies outside that goal into ONE red question on the goal, and that question blocks the goal's Done until he grants it. He grants them together or not at all, which is what "for now" covers.

WHY IT IS BETTER THAN A LIST: a list of exceptions drifts and becomes a hiding place, while a question he answers at the moment of closing cannot. Today the same information is given to him by hand: on 2026-10-06 four of eleven reds in a full run were old debts that claude-windows had to explain in a post.

WHAT COUNTS AS OUTSIDE THE GOAL: every suite that is not one of the goal suites, which goal/G8.6 now settles from his words, an item suites being the test files its own commits changed.

items.title: Files touched per item — the list of files an item's commits changed, kept by the desk and approved by Andy
items.box:
FILES TOUCHED PER ITEM

Andy, 2026-10-09, in desk/G0.0, answering cw's question "make files-touched an explicit field in G8.1, replacing the hand-written list at claim-done?": "Yes. cw: add it to the appropriate goal, and make sure that the file list needs my approval"

WHAT IT REPLACES: the list an agent writes by hand in the item chat at claim-done (Andy, 2026-10-03). desk.js holds no files-touched field today.

WHY ITS OWN ITEM AND NOT goal/G8.1: G8.1 keeps one row per test; this is one list per item. The goal box names it under WHAT IT KEEPS: "which core files were touched and by whom".

REQUIRED, his: the file list needs his approval.
